content: 1. Women diagnosed with postpartum endometritis were treated with various antibiotic regimens, including aztreonam combined with clindamycin versus other regimens. The quality of evidence was rated as very low, with critical importance. The study contributing to the pooled effect had significant design limitations, and the confidence interval was wide, crossing the line of no effect. Additionally, the sample size was small, and there were few events reported. 2. The WHO recommendations for the prevention and treatment of maternal peripartum infections included evidence on the use of antibiotics with longer versus shorter half-lives of the same agent for postpartum endometritis. The quality of evidence was low, with critical importance. The studies contributing to the pooled effect had design limitations, and the confidence interval was wide, crossing the line of no effect. The sample size was small, and there were few events. 3. The use of metronidazole combined with gentamicin versus other antibiotic regimens for postpartum endometritis was evaluated. The quality of evidence was very low, with critical importance. The analysis was based on one study with design limitations. The confidence interval was wide, crossing the line of no effect, and the sample size was small, with few events reported. 4. Once-daily versus thrice-daily gentamicin regimens for postpartum endometritis were compared. The quality of evidence was moderate, with critical importance. Most of the studies contributing to the pooled effect had design limitations. The confidence interval was wide, crossing the line of no effect, and there were few events reported. 5. Continued oral antibiotic treatment following an intravenous course for postpartum endometritis was assessed. The quality of evidence was very low, with critical importance. The studies contributing to the pooled effect had design limitations. The confidence interval was wide, crossing the line of no effect, and the sample size was small, with few events reported. In some cases, no events were observed. 6. Antibiotic regimens with poor versus good activity against penicillinase-resistant bacteria for postpartum endometritis were evaluated. The quality of evidence was low, with critical importance. The studies contributing to the pooled effect had design limitations. The confidence interval was wide, crossing the line of no effect, and the sample size was small, with few events reported. 7. Oral ofloxacin combined with clindamycin versus intravenous clindamycin combined with gentamicin for postpartum endometritis was compared. The quality of evidence was very low, with critical importance. The analysis was based on one study with design limitations. The confidence interval was wide, crossing the line of no effect, and the sample size was small, with few events reported.
